title: Theology surpasses the other sciences in certainty, both in the object and in the habit of faith
pass_a_gloss: Hence Theology surpasses all remaining sciences in certainty. Those rest on human reason which can be deceived and is liable to error. Theology reclines on God truth, who can neither be deceived nor deceive. Many doubt theological truths; principles and conclusions seem less certain than human sciences. That does not hinder them from being in themselves most certain — as sun does not cease most splendid though blind or bleary either not at all or only obscurely perceive its light. When we set Theology more certain than other sciences, we do not mean certainty only from object side. Things God revealed are not only most certain in themselves, but through habit of faith and Theology can be known more certainly than any truths known by light of reason alone. So one strengthened in faith and science of divine things is more certain and more persuaded of divine truths than of any other truth. Habit of faith and Theology in itself and from own species excels in certainty the habit of merely natural sciences — though not all equally participate that habit; firmer in one, less firm in another.
pass_b_english: Hence it comes about that theology surpasses all the remaining sciences in certainty. For those rest on human reason, which can be deceived and is liable to error. But theology reclines upon the truth of God, who can neither be deceived nor deceive. Many indeed waver about theological truths, and to them the principles and conclusions of theology seem less certain than the things handed down in the human sciences. But that does not hinder them from being in themselves most certain — just as the sun does not cease to be most splendid, though the blind and the bleary-eyed either do not perceive its light at all, or perceive it only obscurely.

But here it must be noticed that when we set theology as more certain than the other sciences, we do not so understand it as if that certainty were only on the side of the object. For the things which God has revealed are not only most certain in themselves, but can also be known more certainly through the habit of faith and of theology than any truths known through the light of reason alone. So that one who is strengthened in faith and in the science of divine things is more certain, and more persuaded, concerning the divine truths than he is concerning any other truth. And thus the habit of faith and of theology, in itself and from its own species, excels in certainty the habit of the merely natural sciences — although not all participate that habit equally, and it is firmer in one person and less firm in another.
source_text:
XXXI. Unde fit ut Theologia certitudine superet reliquas omnes scientias. Siquidem illae nituntur ratione humana, quae falli potest, et est errori obnoxia. Sed Theologia recumbit in veritatem Dei, qui nec falli, nec fallere potest. Multi quidem circa veritates Theologicas addubitant, iisque Theologiae principia, et conclusiones minus certa videntur, quam ea quae traduntur in scientiis humanis. Sed id non obstat quo minus in se sint certissima: sicut Sol non desinit esse splendidissimus, licet caeci et lippientes lucem ejus, aut omnino non, aut obscure tantum percipiant.

XXXII. Verum hic animadvertendum, quum ponimus Theologiam certiorem esse aliis scientiis, nos id ita non intelligere, quasi certitudo illa solum esset ex parte objecti. Etenim illa quae Deus revelavit, non tantum sunt in se certissima, sed etiam per habitum fidei, et Theologiae certius cognosci possunt, quam ullae veritates per solum lumen rationis notae. Ita ut qui in fide et rerum divinarum scientia roboratus est, certior sit, et magis persuasus de veritatibus divinis, quam sit de ulla alia veritate. Atque sic fidei et Theologiae habitus, in se et ex propria specie, certitudine antecellit habitus scientiarum mere naturalium, licet omnes non aequaliter participent illum habitum, et sit in uno firmior, in alio vero minus firmus.
